sections.body_md:
On a positive definite quadratic, steepest descent with exact line search has a linear rate that depends only on the shape of the Hessian. Let \(\kappa\) be the ratio of the largest eigenvalue to the smallest. The excess of the objective over its minimum is multiplied, at every step, by a factor no larger than \(((\kappa - 1)/(\kappa + 1))^2\).

The square is there because the excess equals half the squared \(A\)-norm of the error. The \(A\)-norm of the error contracts by the unsquared quotient \((\kappa - 1)/(\kappa + 1)\). Squaring that quotient produces the factor on the excess. When \(\kappa = 1\), the factor is zero: the level sets are spheres and one exact steepest step finishes the problem. As \(\kappa\) grows, the quotient grows toward one and the guarantee becomes slower. A badly stretched ellipse is exactly a large condition number.

The bound is a worst-case statement over starting points. A lucky start on the long axis can do better. The factor cannot be improved in general, because there are starts that meet it. It is also a statement about this algorithm. A method that builds conjugate directions replaces \(\kappa\) by a milder function of \(\kappa\) and keeps a linear rate with a smaller factor.

sections.heading: Key equations
sections.body_md:
With \(\kappa = \lambda_{\max}(A)/\lambda_{\min}(A)\),
\[
f(x^+) - f^\star \le \left(\frac{\kappa - 1}{\kappa + 1}\right)^2 \bigl(f(x) - f^\star\bigr).
\]
The unsquared quotient bounds the error in the \(A\)-norm.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.body_md:
Take \(\kappa = 3/2\). The unsquared quotient is \((1/2) / (5/2) = 1/5\). The factor on the excess is the square of that quotient.

The hoist factor is 0.04. An excess of \(50\) would be guaranteed to fall to at most \(2\) at the next exact steepest step. The same eigenvalues in the opposite order give the same ratio, because \(\kappa\) uses the larger over the smaller. Forgetting the square would have left the factor \(0.2\), which is the contraction of the \(A\)-norm error rather than of the excess.

sections.heading: Common pitfalls
sections.body_md: Dropping the square is the arithmetic error that confuses the two norms. The excess carries the square. The \(A\)-norm error carries the unsquared quotient. A second slip is to use the sum of the eigenvalues in place of their ratio. Two Hessians with the same trace can have very different condition numbers. A third is to treat a factor close to one as a fast rate. Closer to one is slower. A fourth is to apply the factor to a step that is not exact steepest descent. The bound is proved for that pair of choices. A fixed short step has a different estimate.

sections.heading: Where this leads
sections.body_md: Conjugate gradients keep a linear rate and improve the factor to a function of \(\sqrt{\kappa}\) rather than of \(\kappa\). Heavy-ball momentum uses the same condition number to choose the weight on the previous step, and on a quadratic that weight beats the steepest-descent factor. Both methods are later because they start from the rate this bound makes visible.
